title: There is an unborn
hook: there is an unborn, unbecome, unmade; were there not, there'd be no escape

segments.voice: Yesterday: Visakha's wet hair at midday, and your line, a hundred dear, a hundred sorrows. Did you hold someone dear with an open hand? Today closes a week, with a short saying about what isn't made. Day six hundred twenty-three.

Everything you've ever touched was born, or made, or put together. Your phone. Your house. Your body. Your mood this morning. Every one of them came from causes, and every one of them will come apart. That's the whole teaching of impermanence, which you've heard many times on this path. And it raises a hard question. If everything is made, and everything comes apart, is there anything at all that isn't? Is there a way out of the making? In the eighth and last chapter of the Udana, the Buddha answers with four words that start with un. Today: there is an unborn.
screen: `EVERYTHING YOU'VE TOUCHED WAS MADE.` → `EVERYTHING MADE COMES APART.` → `IS THERE A WAY OUT?`

segments.voice: The setting is a talk on nibbana to the monks. And here's the saying, as close as we can come. There is, monks, an unborn, an unbecome, an unmade, an unconditioned. If there were not this unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned, no escape would be known from the born, the become, the made, the conditioned. But because there is, an escape is known. Notice where the weight falls: on two small words, there is. Not it might be, not we hope. The text doesn't describe the unborn at all. It argues for it, from the escape: if there were only the made, there'd be no way out of it. The fact that the path leads somewhere shows there's somewhere to arrive. How do traditions read it? Theravada teachers generally read the unborn as nibbana itself, not a self, not a soul, not a creator, but the unconditioned. Other schools have drawn on the passage in their own ways. The text itself simply says, there is. Look back at the week. Nanda's pull home. Meghiya not yet ripe. The elephant read whole. Moths at the lamp. Suppavasa giving. Visakha's hundred sorrows. Every one of them was about the born and the made. Today, the Udana points past them.
screen: `A TALK ON NIBBANA.` · `UNBORN, UNBECOME, UNMADE.` · `IF THERE WERE NOT, NO ESCAPE.` · `IT SAYS WHAT IT ISN'T.` · then, large: `THERE IS AN UNBORN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest in stillness. Sit and settle. Notice how everything in your experience is moving: the breath, sounds, sensations, thoughts arriving and leaving. Don't chase any of them. Don't try to find the unborn, either; it isn't a thing to find. Just let the movement go on, and rest as the quiet that notices it. If a thought comes, let it be one more passing thing. The bell holds the time.
There is an unborn. The Udana's saying on nibbana: an unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned; because it is, there is an escape from the made. Today's word.
Your line: there is an unborn. Today, when something you depend on changes or breaks, remember that the Buddha pointed to something that doesn't. Day six hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: The saying on the unborn is studied in Theravada teaching on nibbana and is quoted by teachers of many Buddhist schools; it also appears in the Itivuttaka (Iti 43).

match.prompt: there is an unborn: tap the pairs.

myth: the saying describes the unborn in detail
every word is a negative; it says what it isn't, and that it is.
the saying argues from the possibility of escape
if there were no unborn, no escape from the born would be known.
Theravada teachers generally read the unborn as a creator god
they generally read it as nibbana, the unconditioned, not a self or a creator.

fork.setup: you're a monk at the Buddha's talk on nibbana. you ask: if everything is made and comes apart, how can there be a way out? what does the saying answer?
options: there is no way out; accept it.
there is an unborn, unmade; because there is, there is an escape.
the way out is to be reborn in heaven.
fork.reveal: the Udana says there is an unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned, and that because there is, escape from the made is known.

original.note: Pali ajata: unborn. the saying begins atthi bhikkhave ajatam: there is, monks, an unborn.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism says everything is impermanent, full stop.
what it means: everything made is impermanent; the Udana also says there is an unborn, unmade, and that's why there is an escape.
what a scholar hears: Udana 8.3 (ajatam abhutam akatam asankhatam) is paralleled in Itivuttaka 43; its four negatives are often cited when teachers speak of nibbana.

notes: Udana 8.3 paraphrased closely ('as close as we can come'). Strong's 1902 translation exists but is not on the validator list.

The reading of the unborn varies across schools; the script states the general Theravada reading and says other schools draw on it 'in their own ways' without naming them. A Keeper may want to add specifics.

Audit (second sample): removed the unsourced superlatives ('one of the deepest passages', 'one of the canon's most quoted'), and cut the says-only-what-it-isn't angle, which day 624 (Udana 8.1) is built on; today now centers the saying's argument from escape.
